case_info.scenario: A 51-year-old previously healthy man was admitted with severe neck pain for 6 days. In the past month, he felt neck stiffness, accompanied by swelling and persistent dull pain of the upper anterior chest wall, which could be transiently relieved by taking oral ibuprofen. Six days before admission, the patient’s neck stiffness transited to an endurable dull ache. When turning his head, there was severe burning pain in the posterior neck and occiput, followed immediately by an electric shocklike numbness on ipsilateral side tongue, which led to a forced head position. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine with gadolinium on admission revealed signal abnormality in C1/C2 vertebrae (Figure 1A). In the past 3 days, with the intensification of neck pain, the patient found pustules on both hands, which gradually increased. He had no history of tobacco, alcohol, or drug misuse. On examination, he was afebrile. There was tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation, upper neck, post aurem, and occiput. Multiple pustules were seen in the palm and back of both hands (Figure 1B). Complete blood cell count and liver and kidney function yielded normal results, except for elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 93 mm/h and C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 5.5 mg/dL (to convert to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10). Results of workup for rheumatic and infectious disease, including antinuclear, antineutrophil cytoplasmic and anticardiolipin antibodies, human leukocyte antigen B27, repeated blood cultures, rapid plasma reagin test, Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, brucella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and rickettsial antibodies, were all negative. Cell count, protein, and glucose in cerebrospinal fluid were normal. Cultures of cerebrospinal fluid revealed no organisms. Whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography revealed no malignancy.

case_info.caption: Abnormal enhancement of C1/C2 vertebrae with prevertebral and retrodental tissue as well as of the anterior vertebrae at C4/C5 with hyperostotic anterior osteophytes on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and multiple pustules on the palm (B).
case_info.explanation: D. Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. An association betweenCSF2RA,NOD2,MEGF6, andADAM5genes and the predisposition of SAPHO syndrome has been established.5Elevated serum IgG4 and some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL) 6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-23 and endothelin-1, have been described in patients with SAPHO syndrome.6In laboratory tests, and features of an active inflammatory process (accelerated ESR, elevated CRP) are observed.7 The diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome is based on fulfilling at least 1 of the criteria described by Kahn and Kahn,8which include (1) chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, usually sterile, spine may be involved, with or without skin lesions, (2) acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis associated with any of the following: palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), pustular psoriasis, or severe acne, and (3) any sterile osteitis associated with any of the following: PPP, pustular psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, or severe acne. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. Current treatment options for SAPHO syndrome include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, and biologics.10 After oral etoricoxib and prednisolone treatment, neck pain and pustules gradually subsided and ESR and CRP decreased. The patient has remained clinically stable at 6-month follow-up. Clinicians should be aware of this unusual syndrome to avoid misdiagnosis (tumor/infection), unnecessary surgery, and antibiotic therapy.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

case_info.caption: Abnormal enhancement of C1/C2 vertebrae with prevertebral and retrodental tissue as well as of the anterior vertebrae at C4/C5 with hyperostotic anterior osteophytes on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and multiple pustules on the palm (B).
case_info.explanation: D. Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. An association betweenCSF2RA,NOD2,MEGF6, andADAM5genes and the predisposition of SAPHO syndrome has been established.5Elevated serum IgG4 and some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL) 6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-23 and endothelin-1, have been described in patients with SAPHO syndrome.6In laboratory tests, and features of an active inflammatory process (accelerated ESR, elevated CRP) are observed.7 The diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome is based on fulfilling at least 1 of the criteria described by Kahn and Kahn,8which include (1) chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, usually sterile, spine may be involved, with or without skin lesions, (2) acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis associated with any of the following: palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), pustular psoriasis, or severe acne, and (3) any sterile osteitis associated with any of the following: PPP, pustular psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, or severe acne. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. Current treatment options for SAPHO syndrome include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, and biologics.10 After oral etoricoxib and prednisolone treatment, neck pain and pustules gradually subsided and ESR and CRP decreased. The patient has remained clinically stable at 6-month follow-up. Clinicians should be aware of this unusual syndrome to avoid misdiagnosis (tumor/infection), unnecessary surgery, and antibiotic therapy.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

[Clinical case]
A 51-year-old previously healthy man was admitted with severe neck pain for 6 days. In the past month, he felt neck stiffness, accompanied by swelling and persistent dull pain of the upper anterior chest wall, which could be transiently relieved by taking oral ibuprofen. Six days before admission, the patient’s neck stiffness transited to an endurable dull ache. When turning his head, there was severe burning pain in the posterior neck and occiput, followed immediately by an electric shocklike numbness on ipsilateral side tongue, which led to a forced head position. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine with gadolinium on admission revealed signal abnormality in C1/C2 vertebrae (Figure 1A). In the past 3 days, with the intensification of neck pain, the patient found pustules on both hands, which gradually increased. He had no history of tobacco, alcohol, or drug misuse. On examination, he was afebrile. There was tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation, upper neck, post aurem, and occiput. Multiple pustules were seen in the palm and back of both hands (Figure 1B). Complete blood cell count and liver and kidney function yielded normal results, except for elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 93 mm/h and C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 5.5 mg/dL (to convert to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10). Results of workup for rheumatic and infectious disease, including antinuclear, antineutrophil cytoplasmic and anticardiolipin antibodies, human leukocyte antigen B27, repeated blood cultures, rapid plasma reagin test, Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, brucella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and rickettsial antibodies, were all negative. Cell count, protein, and glucose in cerebrospinal fluid were normal. Cultures of cerebrospinal fluid revealed no organisms. Whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography revealed no malignancy.

case_info.caption: Abnormal enhancement of C1/C2 vertebrae with prevertebral and retrodental tissue as well as of the anterior vertebrae at C4/C5 with hyperostotic anterior osteophytes on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and multiple pustules on the palm (B).
case_info.explanation: D. Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. An association betweenCSF2RA,NOD2,MEGF6, andADAM5genes and the predisposition of SAPHO syndrome has been established.5Elevated serum IgG4 and some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL) 6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-23 and endothelin-1, have been described in patients with SAPHO syndrome.6In laboratory tests, and features of an active inflammatory process (accelerated ESR, elevated CRP) are observed.7 The diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome is based on fulfilling at least 1 of the criteria described by Kahn and Kahn,8which include (1) chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, usually sterile, spine may be involved, with or without skin lesions, (2) acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis associated with any of the following: palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), pustular psoriasis, or severe acne, and (3) any sterile osteitis associated with any of the following: PPP, pustular psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, or severe acne. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. Current treatment options for SAPHO syndrome include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, and biologics.10 After oral etoricoxib and prednisolone treatment, neck pain and pustules gradually subsided and ESR and CRP decreased. The patient has remained clinically stable at 6-month follow-up. Clinicians should be aware of this unusual syndrome to avoid misdiagnosis (tumor/infection), unnecessary surgery, and antibiotic therapy.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

}

case_info.scenario: A 51-year-old previously healthy man was admitted with severe neck pain for 6 days. In the past month, he felt neck stiffness, accompanied by swelling and persistent dull pain of the upper anterior chest wall, which could be transiently relieved by taking oral ibuprofen. Six days before admission, the patient’s neck stiffness transited to an endurable dull ache. When turning his head, there was severe burning pain in the posterior neck and occiput, followed immediately by an electric shocklike numbness on ipsilateral side tongue, which led to a forced head position. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine with gadolinium on admission revealed signal abnormality in C1/C2 vertebrae (Figure 1A). In the past 3 days, with the intensification of neck pain, the patient found pustules on both hands, which gradually increased. He had no history of tobacco, alcohol, or drug misuse. On examination, he was afebrile. There was tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation, upper neck, post aurem, and occiput. Multiple pustules were seen in the palm and back of both hands (Figure 1B). Complete blood cell count and liver and kidney function yielded normal results, except for elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 93 mm/h and C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 5.5 mg/dL (to convert to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10). Results of workup for rheumatic and infectious disease, including antinuclear, antineutrophil cytoplasmic and anticardiolipin antibodies, human leukocyte antigen B27, repeated blood cultures, rapid plasma reagin test, Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, brucella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and rickettsial antibodies, were all negative. case_info.caption: Abnormal enhancement of C1/C2 vertebrae with prevertebral and retrodental tissue as well as of the anterior vertebrae at C4/C5 with hyperostotic anterior osteophytes on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and multiple pustules on the palm (B).
case_info.explanation: D. Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. An association betweenCSF2RA,NOD2,MEGF6, andADAM5genes and the predisposition of SAPHO syndrome has been established.5Elevated serum IgG4 and some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL) 6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-23 and endothelin-1, have been described in patients with SAPHO syndrome.6In laboratory tests, and features of an active inflammatory process (accelerated ESR, elevated CRP) are observed.7 The diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome is based on fulfilling at least 1 of the criteria described by Kahn and Kahn,8which include (1) chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, usually sterile, spine may be involved, with or without skin lesions, (2) acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis associated with any of the following: palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), pustular psoriasis, or severe acne, and (3) any sterile osteitis associated with any of the following: PPP, pustular psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, or severe acne. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. Current treatment options for SAPHO syndrome include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, and biologics.10 After oral etoricoxib and prednisolone treatment, neck pain and pustules gradually subsided and ESR and CRP decreased. The patient has remained clinically stable at 6-month follow-up. Clinicians should be aware of this unusual syndrome to avoid misdiagnosis (tumor/infection), unnecessary surgery, and antibiotic therapy.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.caption: Abnormal enhancement of C1/C2 vertebrae with prevertebral and retrodental tissue as well as of the anterior vertebrae at C4/C5 with hyperostotic anterior osteophytes on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and multiple pustules on the palm (B).
case_info.explanation: D. Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. An association betweenCSF2RA,NOD2,MEGF6, andADAM5genes and the predisposition of SAPHO syndrome has been established.5Elevated serum IgG4 and some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL) 6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-23 and endothelin-1, have been described in patients with SAPHO syndrome.6In laboratory tests, and features of an active inflammatory process (accelerated ESR, elevated CRP) are observed.7 The diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome is based on fulfilling at least 1 of the criteria described by Kahn and Kahn,8which include (1) chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, usually sterile, spine may be involved, with or without skin lesions, (2) acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis associated with any of the following: palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), pustular psoriasis, or severe acne, and (3) any sterile osteitis associated with any of the following: PPP, pustular psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, or severe acne. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. Current treatment options for SAPHO syndrome include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, and biologics.10 After oral etoricoxib and prednisolone treatment, neck pain and pustules gradually subsided and ESR and CRP decreased. The patient has remained clinically stable at 6-month follow-up. Clinicians should be aware of this unusual syndrome to avoid misdiagnosis (tumor/infection), unnecessary surgery, and antibiotic therapy.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Currently reachable stages (Hitchcock ordering rules): CONSIDER, INFORM, PROPOSE, RECOMMEND
You MUST pick a stage from this list.

Initiating treatment with high-dose NSAIDs is a standard first-line therapy for SAPHO, and early rheumatology consultation is recommended for severe or refractory cases to coordinate potential steroid or DMARD use, aiming to control inflammation and prevent structural damage. The clinician's plan correctly integrates acute symptom management with specialist oversight, aligning with best practices for this complex, non-infectious inflammatory disorder.
  evidence_gaps:  ['Specific MRI description of hyperostosis or osteosclerosis to definitively meet SAPHO imaging criteria', 'Formal diagnostic criteria for SAPHO syndrome (e.g., Benhamou criteria) application to this case']

Dialogue so far (each medical turn is annotated with the move that produced it — this is

While atypical locations can raise concerns for alternative diagnoses, the absence of systemic infection signs and the specific imaging findings align more closely with SAPHO than with osteomyelitis or spondylodiscitis. Differentiating between these would typically rely on clinical context and imaging findings, which here favor SAPHO due to its characteristic presentation and negative infectious screen. To solidify the diagnosis and guide therapy, I would ask you to justify the specific imaging findings on the MRI—what does the signal abnormality at C1/C2 actually look like, and are there features like hyperostosis, osteosclerosis, or joint involvement that are classic for SAPHO?

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 51-year-old previously healthy man was admitted with severe neck pain for 6 days. In the past month, he felt neck stiffness, accompanied by swelling and persistent dull pain of the upper anterior chest wall, which could be transiently relieved by taking oral ibuprofen. Six days before admission, the patient’s neck stiffness transited to an endurable dull ache. When turning his head, there was severe burning pain in the posterior neck and occiput, followed immediately by an electric shocklike numbness on ipsilateral side tongue, which led to a forced head position. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine with gadolinium on admission revealed signal abnormality in C1/C2 vertebrae (Figure 1A). In the past 3 days, with the intensification of neck pain, the patient found pustules on both hands, which gradually increased. He had no history of tobacco, alcohol, or drug misuse. On examination, he was afebrile. There was tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation, upper neck, post aurem, and occiput. Multiple pustules were seen in the palm and back of both hands (Figure 1B). Complete blood cell count and liver and kidney function yielded normal results, except for elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 93 mm/h and C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 5.5 mg/dL (to convert to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10). Results of workup for rheumatic and infectious disease, including antinuclear, antineutrophil cytoplasmic and anticardiolipin antibodies, human leukocyte antigen B27, repeated blood cultures, rapid plasma reagin test, Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, brucella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and rickettsial antibodies, were all negative. Cell count, protein, and glucose in cerebrospinal fluid were normal. Cultures of cerebrospinal fluid revealed no organisms. Whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography revealed no malignancy.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Stage: INFORM | Locution: ask_justify(fact)
Apply this deliberation move in your response.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

This condition correlates with the observed symptoms and imaging abnormalities. The negative results for infectious and rheumatic diseases further support this diagnosis. Thus, treatment should focus on addressing SAPHO syndrome.

I agree that SAPHO syndrome is a strong consideration given the constellation of findings. However, could you justify why you are focusing on the C1/C2 abnormality as the primary osteitis, and how you would specifically differentiate it from other causes of osteomyelitis or spondylodiscitis at that atypical location?

The focal osteitis at C1/C2, along with the skin manifestations and negative infectious workup, strongly suggests SAPHO syndrome. While atypical locations can raise concerns for alternative diagnoses, the absence of systemic infection signs and the specific imaging findings align more closely with SAPHO than with osteomyelitis or spondylodiscitis. Differentiating between these would typically rely on clinical context and imaging findings, which here favor SAPHO due to its characteristic presentation and negative infectious screen. I believe we should proceed with management aimed at treating SAPHO syndrome.

Your justification is sound, and I agree that the clinical and imaging picture points strongly toward SAPHO syndrome. To solidify the diagnosis and guide therapy, I would ask you to justify the specific imaging findings on the MRI—what does the signal abnormality at C1/C2 actually look like, and are there features like hyperostosis, osteosclerosis, or joint involvement that are classic for SAPHO?

The MRI findings at C1/C2 show abnormal enhancement consistent with osteitis rather than typical features of infectious processes like osteomyelitis. In SAPHO syndrome, hyperostosis and the specific location of the lesions can manifest atypically, which is supported by the pustular skin lesions. Given the complete negative infectious workup and the clinical picture, I still firmly believe that the management should focus on SAPHO syndrome as the diagnosis here.

I agree that the evidence strongly points away from infection and toward SAPHO. To finalize the diagnostic criteria and plan initial treatment, could you justify the choice of first-line therapy for SAPHO syndrome in this acute setting? For instance, would you start with high-dose NSAIDs, corticosteroids, or consider a disease-modifying agent given the severity of the spinal involvement?

In this acute setting, I would initiate treatment with high-dose NSAIDs to manage the inflammation and pain associated with SAPHO syndrome. Depending on the patient's response, we may consider corticosteroids if there is inadequate relief, especially given the severity of spinal involvement. The choice of treatment will be tailored based on the patient's presentation and progress. I still believe SAPHO syndrome is the most appropriate diagnosis, and we should proceed accordingly.

That's a reasonable stepwise approach, starting with NSAIDs. Given the severe cervical involvement, I'd also consider a baseline rheumatology consult to coordinate potential steroid use or DMARDs early if NSAIDs fail, to prevent structural complications.
